🚀 Feature
Merge torch.mean and torch.var kernels on GPU.
Motivation
torch.var GPU kernel launch config does not scale with larger reduction size. Meanwhile, torch.mean performs really well and the math are similar (torch.var uses welford so it is pratically the same single pass reduction).
At larger scale I am seeing 100x speed up.
Pitch
We should figure out a reduction op API so we can support different math in our reduction op. That would enable us to merge torch.mean and torch.var kernel launch configurations.
Alternatives
We can definitely improve torch.var kernel separately, since it has slightly more complicated math, we might expect it requires different heuristics than the one used in torch.mean. But this might not be that much of a problem.
Additional context
I have some monkey benchmark. Comparing torch.mean torch.var and my test kernel welford (which does a mean/var on contiguous dimension)
I have a 2d input tensor and does reduction on each dimension separately.

Motivation
Launching a FusionGroup for a JIT LSTM cell takes ~40us CPU time, as reported by the autograd profiler. This is not good because the kernel itself takes < 10us CUDA time and could probably be faster. After seeing nothing noticeably wrong with the JIT, I am looking into core performance overheads.
Methodology
Performance is measured with gbenchmark microbenchmarks: https://github.com/pytorch/benchmark/tree/master/timing/cpp2. Here is some sample output that motivates many of the below tasks.
Investigations


 [#12824] Speed up torch.empty({0}). It is implemented by making a tensor and then calling resize_({0}); that resize_ should be a no-op but it takes 300ns.


 [#12841][#13590] get_device is slow because it does two dispatches. It's used for the DeviceGuard(tensor) ctor.


 [#12841] is_cuda is slow. It's used pretty commonly, most notably in DeviceGuard.


 [#13185 @zou3519] rewrite torch.as_strided.


 [#13267 @zou3519] speed up tensor.storage_offset(). as_strided is 100ns slower with/without a storage_offset argument (the lack of presense of one calls tensor.storage_offset()).


 [#13411 @zou3519] stop allocating and throwing away StorageImpl during torch.as_strided


 [probably done @zou3519] investigate torch.as_strided perf (it shouldn't be that much slower than just creating an empty tensor because we're setting fields on the new tensor).


 [#13330 @zou3519 ] tensor.options() takes 50ns.


 [#13580 @zou3519] I think Variable::Impl's ctor constructs an empty StorageImpl, which costs like 200ns...


 [#13649 @zou3519] Use at::SmallVector for TensorImpl's sizes and strides. This saves some time while allocating a tensor by avoiding dynamic allocations


 [#13785 @zou3519] Speed up at::empty by avoiding DeviceGuard. at::empty_cuda now only does 1 DeviceGuard.


 [#13785] Speed up torch.resize_(...), which is important in creating tensors of non-empty size. Killed resizing logic in torch.empty. It no longer performs a resize; this results in a small speedup.


 [done #13974] Use fewer DeviceGuards in common ops #13269 #13741 motivation timings


 [#13974 DeviceGuard is no longer a problem!] DeviceGuard takes 300ns (before #12841) 100ns 200ns. It should ideally only perform a cudaGetDevice and be 34ns. Also, it would be great if we could cache a thread-local device but that may lead to consistency issues. (bad idea). A typical JIT LSTM does 11100 DeviceGuard at 100ns, which is 1.1ms overhead. cudnn does forward + bwd in a total of 17ms.


 [open] Library overhead: it takes 4us from an at::mm call until a gemm kernel begins launching. It shouldn't need to take that long; we need to allocate the output tensor but that should be < 2us.


 [in progress @zou3519 ] at::detail::infer_type takes 500-700ns typically (35ns when run in a tight loop). This is pretty bad. Should run experiment to cache type (in a hacky way) on TensorImpl and see if that improves the timing or not


 [open] eliminate tensor.type().scalarType() idiom in favor of tensor.scalarType or tensor.dtype(). Not sure if this is actually perf critical


 [open] Investigate THCCachingAllocator performance.


 [open] investigate caching device on TensorImpl #12934


 [open] Look into overhead of creating a Variable. We currently create a StorageImpl, then use make_tensor, and finally use as_variable; as_variable seems pretty expensive. LSTM forward + backward creates 1100 tensors at 400ns variable overhead each, which is 0.4ms overhead. cudnn does forward + bwd in a total of 17ms.


 [in progress @yf225 #13638] Tensor-Variable merge will get rid of our Variable overhead, leading to significant wins

🚀 Feature
Currently only one _LRScheduler can be used with the same optimizer. It would be great to support using multiple ones simultaneously.
Motivation
It's not uncommon in NLP (see e.g. here) to want to use both StepLR and ReduceLROnPlateau. This isn't possible currently, because StepLR calculates learning rate updates based on what was the initial learning rate, and how many epochs have gone by (see get_lr()). This is all based on the assumption the learning rate hasn't been touched by anything else.
Pitch
This can be fixed by having StepLR,  ExponentialLR (and potentially others) query the optimizer to find out the current learning rate, instead of attempting to work it out what it should be. ReduceLROnPlateau already does this in _reduce_lr().

🐛 Bug
The conv grads computed by https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/grad.py rely on the function _grad_input_padding() (from the same file). _grad_input_padding() raises a ValueError when dilation>1 because  it does not account for dilation when computing its expected input size.
To Reproduce
The following snippet appears to correctly create a grad with respect to the input  via torch.autograd.grad with dilation=2 (stored in grad_input). We should be able to get the same grad by using torch.nn.grad.conv2d_input(), but attempting to do so leads to a ValueError raised by _grad_input_padding() when dilation>1:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
input = torch.randn(1,1,5,5, requires_grad=True)
weight = torch.randn(1,1,3,3, requires_grad=True)
output = F.conv2d(input, weight, dilation=2)
grad_output = torch.randn(output.shape)
grad_input = torch.autograd.grad(output, input, grad_output)
torch.nn.grad.conv2d_input(input.shape, weight, grad_output, dilation=2)
Error message:

File "/home/.../anaconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/grad.py", line 29, in _grad_input_padding
grad_output.size()[2:]))


ValueError: requested an input grad size of [5, 5], but valid sizes range from [3, 3] to [3, 3] (for a grad_output of torch.Size([1, 1]))

As we would expect with a 5x5 input, 3x3 kernel, and dilation=2, the output size is [1,1]. According to _grad_input_padding(), the only possible input size was [3,3]. I believe the fix is to make _grad_input_padding() account for dilation. In this case, accounting for dilation would allow this function to know that  [5,5] is the only acceptable input size.

test_pstrf tests pstrf on positive definite matrices instead of testing on positive semi definite matrices. This caused us to not catch errors like #12435 .
The culprit is this segment of code:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/test/test_torch.py#L5379-L5381
Removing this segment produces errors about the input matrix being rank deficient. Rank deficiency for a real symmetric matrix is when at least one of the eigenvalues is zero. This scenario is plausible for positive semi definite matrices by definition.
cc: @zou3519

torch.nn.L1Loss()'s parameter reduction doesn't work if b = net(a).
b = net(a)
l = torch.nn.L1Loss(reduction='elementwise_mean')
l(a, b) # wrong, it's summation 


To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

datadim = 33


class BugNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(BugNet, self).__init__()
        self.output = nn.Linear(datadim, datadim)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.output(x)


a = torch.ones((4, 33))
bug = BugNet()
b = bug(a)

loss_fn1 = nn.L1Loss(reduction='sum')
loss_fn2 = nn.L1Loss(reduction='elementwise_mean')
elementwise_mean_loss = lambda x, x_out: torch.mean(torch.abs(x-x_out.view_as(x)))

print(loss_fn1(a, b))  # 127.6617, True
print(loss_fn2(a, b))  # 127.6617, False
print(loss_fn2(b, a))  # 0.9671, True
print(elementwise_mean_loss(a, b))  # 0.9671, True

Background. Here is the current state of RAII stream/device handling in PyTorch and Caffe2.
PyTorch has the following implementations:

DeviceGuard, is a class for managing cudaSetDevice/cudaGetDevice calls. It is accessible from the CPU library, and handles cross CPU-GPU calls using a table of function pointers in CUDAHooksInterface.
CUDAGuard is a CUDA library only class that manages both device and stream. Desired stream is identified via the CUDAStream object.
StreamGuard is a CUDA library only class in c10d that is basically an exact copy of CUDAGuard, but worse (it calls legacy THC APIs)

Caffe2 has the following implementations:

DeviceGuard, is a CUDA library only class that wraps calls to CaffeCudaSetDevice/CaffeCudaGetDevice. The primary difference here is that these functions are controlled by an option FLAGS_caffe2_cuda_full_device_control which, when true, assumes that we can maintain a shadow thread_local variable that accurately reflects what the current CUDA device is.

Requirements.

The guard must be device agnostic in some way

Caffe2 supports more backends than just CPU and CUDA. DeviceGuard must be able to handle these cases.
Stream identification should be done as an int (or a small wrapper struct around the int), and not as a class, so that we can represent streams of different device types uniformly.


The guard must be dispatchable at both compile time and runtime:

The most common call sites for device switching (SwitchToDevice) in Caffe2 are in places templatized by a Context parameter; thus, Caffe2 knows at compile-time which device guard it wants; the only requirement is that the device guards for different devices have a uniform interface (which can be accessed from Context). Thus, it is not necessary to be run time device agnostic.
Due to architectural decisions in PyTorch, PyTorch requires the ability to call a DeviceGuard from CPU code. This is because at the time we set device correctly, we have not performed dispatch yet, and are in device agnostic code. This is particularly appropriate for composite ops, where we want to change the device once for an entire set of operations, but the top-level of the composite op is backend independent and would work for CPU or CUDA.

It's possible that we could rework how this works, but it would be substantial work.




Performance is important, because DeviceGuard is called on entry to every operation.

We don't want a virtual dispatch to a function which itself performs a non-inlineable function call; this is why DeviceGuard hard codes function pointers to get_device/set_device, etc. (c.f. design discussion between Sam Gross and Peter Goldsborough.) Maintaining this design while being device agnostic may be a bit more difficult.


The device agnostic interface should live in c10.
It must be possible to set the stream/device without relying on RAII. This keeps API parity with Caffe2's current SwitchToDevice()

@apaszke found that this commit (1178851) is a major culprit in the ~6% perf regression we've seen on here: https://apaszke.github.io/pytorch-perf-hud/.
The above commit makes a bunch of changes, most of which are probably not relevant.  In particular the commit message mentions:
1) Most usages are replaced by at::empty.
2) native_tensor has its namespace function removed
3) Type.tensor(sizes, strides) becomes at::empty_strided(sizes, strides).



is certainly not relevant.


or 3) may be, it's likely that the dispatch is slower for at::empty(...) or at::empty_strided(...) than Type.tensor(...).  This most of the time shouldn't matter, but it's likely one or more places we changed are along some hot path.  Luckily the changes are pretty much self contained, so it should be possible to find the culprit by just reverting the changes basically file-by-file.


Once the culprit is addressed, we should figure out why the specific function call is slower than Type.tensor.  Is this all TensorOptions overhead?  e.g. before:
Type.tensor(size) would be dispatched directly, whereas now the pattern is:
at::empty(size, Type.options()) -> native::empty(size, Type.options()) -> Type.tensor(size)
Is creating options slow?  Is passing options slow?  Is looking up Type from options slow?
Note also that this has further changed in master.  In particular:

TensorOptions is now smaller, so should pass faster (I think this was changed after this commit)
at::empty now uses backend-specific dispatch instead of dispatching back through Type.

cc @ezyang @bhosmer @smessmer @ljk53 @bdhirsh @ailzhang @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel

Post copied below:
I am trying to pass a set of gpu models to a pool of processes, so something like the example code below:
(torch version 1.0.0.dev20181015)
import torch.multiprocessing as mp
mp.set_start_method('spawn', force=True)
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import time


def run(inpt):
    workers, worker_queue = inpt
    while worker_queue.empty():
        time.sleep(0.1)
    worker_id = worker_queue.get()
    model = workers[worker_id]
    data = torch.rand(5, 10)
    data = data.cuda()
    with torch.no_grad():
        result = model(data)
    worker_queue.put(worker_id)
    return result


def main():
    workers = []
    worker_queue = mp.Manager().Queue()  # mp.Queue()
    for worker_id in range(10):
        worker_model = nn.BatchNorm1d(10)
        worker_model.cuda()
        worker_model.eval()
        workers.append(worker_model)
        worker_queue.put(worker_id)

    pools = mp.Pool(10)

    jobs = [(workers, worker_queue) for _ in range(20)]  # jobs
    result = []
    for res_id, res in enumerate(pools.imap_unordered(run, jobs)):

🚀 Feature
torch.nn.Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1) basically just convert the input as input.flatten(start_dim, end_dim)
Motivation
Let's think that we have code
import torch

a = torch.rand(1024, 100)

model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(100, 50),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(50, 1),
)

print(model(a).shape)
The shape would be torch.Size([1024, 1]), but sometimes it would be more convenient to have a shape torch.Size([1024]) instead. If we had torch.nn.Flatten, we can simply do:
import torch

a = torch.rand(1024, 100)

model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(100, 50),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(50, 1),
    torch.nn.Flatten(start_dim=0)
)

print(model(a).shape)
Also, if we want to do a CNN that has fully connected layers following conv layers, torch.nn.Flatten would also be useful:
import torch

a = torch.rand(1024, 3, 100, 100)

model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 10, 3),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Conv2d(10, 5, 3),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Flatten(),
    torch.nn.Linear(46080, 50),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(50, 1),
)

print(model(a).shape)
Additional context
If the pytorch team think this is a good feature, I will do the PR.
See also: https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/layers/Flatten
